conflicts.point: Whether automated telemetry and feedback loops successfully prevent synthetic error accumulation over long time horizons.

positions.stance: Automated telemetry and real-time tracking successfully detect and repair synthetic errors, preventing long-term data degradation.
Recursive machine training on unverified outputs causes systemic error accumulation and institutional knowledge decay within eighteen months.

conflicts.point: Whether pre-deployment safety gates and accountability structures are necessary safeguards or regulatory bottlenecks.

positions.stance: Pre-deployment committees and regulatory mandates impose bureaucratic delay that harms workers and protects legacy vendors.
Verifiable rollback protocols and named institutional accountability are required before deployment to prevent systemic collapse.

verdicts.conflict: Whether automated telemetry and feedback loops successfully prevent synthetic error accumulation over long time horizons.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions rely on limited or mismatched evidence samples. The accelerationist claim measures short-term sandbox metrics, while the safetyist claim projects long-term systemic failure without empirical proof of inevitability.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Multi-year enterprise case studies measuring error rates and correction overhead past the eighteen-month mark would tip the balance.

verdicts.conflict: Whether pre-deployment safety gates and accountability structures are necessary safeguards or regulatory bottlenecks.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position offers concrete mechanisms like verifiable rollback protocols and named institutional accountability. The accelerationist counter-argument relies on broad assertions of bureaucratic delay without proposing alternative oversight structures.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical proof that lighter oversight structures achieve equal error mitigation without adding administrative delay would flip this verdict.
